doc.title: Loren Schoenberg interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2019

title: Len Garment and the failed first jazz museum
summary: Garment's Nixon arts career and the first national jazz museum project dying.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans

But he was a Brooklyn liberal guy who wound up in the Nixon White House and became a real, I guess what you’d call eminence grise in Washington in the 70s days with Pat Moynihan at the U.N. and was a real culturally, he loved culture. And through the mechanisms of Washington and politics of lobbying and politics he wound up doing a lot of great things. The National Endowments for the Arts and Humanities, which were created during the Nixon administration, excuse me, during the Johnson administration, they were very small. When Nixon got into power he brought Len Garment with him. Len became like the Arts Czar in the Nixon years. And he hired a woman named Nancy Hanks. It was under Nancy Hanks that the endowments went from a few hundred thousand dollars or several hundred thousand — to gazillions of tens of millions. That was Len. Also the Duke Ellington birthday party. So a lot of great things happened with Len. Len had a great sense of humor. He was tagged with going out to solve the problem at Wounded Knee with Russell Means and the Native Americans, he met the chief of the Sioux Nation at which he famously said, “That’s funny, you don’t look Siouxish.” But anyway, he had a great sense of humor, and they laughed when he said it. Well anyway Len had the idea to build a national jazz museum. So he got some money from friends in Washington who loved jazz, and they raised a few hundred thousand dollars and said okay, we’re going to hire someone up in New York, up in Harlem, and then we’re going to somehow get this jazz museum going. Well I heard about this. I knew Len. And I hadn’t been invited to participate and that’s okay, but I heard about it from Stanley Crouch, I heard about it from, I don’t know any number of people I knew saying well we had a meeting on this jazz museum. And okay great. Well to make a long story slightly less long that version of the jazz museum just died. The guy who was leading it, this death by a thousand blows of a 501C3. This consultant, this consultant, and next thing you know the money was gone, they hadn’t raised any money, and the project died. So I knew Len and when he would come to New York we’d meet and just listen to him talk, oh his great stories. He wrote a wonderful book by the way, called Crazy Rhythm, which Saul Bellow wrote a wonderful little blurb on, I strongly recommend it. Anyway, I met with him at the Carlyle once before going to work with Bobby that night, and he said, “You know this jazz museum thing” he said, “it died, but we just got a million dollars from Congress from Ted Stevens.” He was head of appropriations. And we don’t have an organization. I don’t know what to do. Would you, could you recommend someone who could take this on you know. And it wound up that I said well I’ll try it. He said well you can’t do it, you’re doing all these other things, you don’t have time. And I said well I’d like to try.
